pages.text: "I can zoom across this alone!" Leo the know-it-all fox stepped onto the frozen stream. It was frozen solid into a shiny sliding path. He wanted to slide straight to the rock across it.
"Watch. Put your feet like this..." Leo lifted his muzzle and pushed off. Back feet wobbled, front feet wobbled. Thump! He landed on his bottom.
Ppino the rabbit, always first at everything, asked, "Are you okay?" Leo quickly got up and walked off the ice into the snow. "I wasn't going to slide anyway. It's boring."
Ppino slid all the way to the rock across the ice. Leo stood in the snow, fiddling with his orange collar. But his toes kept pointing toward the ice.
Grandma Bear, who ran the lodge, stood at the edge and pointed. Three bottom-shaped marks lay on the ice. One close, one farther, and one near the other side.
"Those are where Ppino fell today. Each fall was a little farther along." Grandma brushed snow from her own bottom to show him. Leo counted the marks quietly. One, two, three.
Leo stepped onto the ice again. He slid, then thump! This time he sprang up and brushed off his bottom. "Brush your bottom—try again!"
Leo's marks on the ice grew to one, two, three, four. On the fifth try, he didn't fall. His hand touched the rock across the stream. "I reached it!" he shouted.
Ppino crossed and stood beside Leo. "One, fall, then brush your bottom! Two, stand ahead of the mark again! Three, try again until it works!" Side by side, they slid.
Ppino gave Leo a big hug. Grandma clapped at the edge. Fall marks aren't shameful. They show how far you've come. Leo laughed and called, "I fell four times earlier! Brush your bottom—try again!"
